title: The Deque Interface: Double-Ended Queues & Stacks
summary: Double-ended queues (addFirst, addLast, pollFirst, pollLast). Why java.util.Stack is a legacy anti-pattern and Deque is the modern stack.
prerequisites: The Queue Contract & FIFO Buffer Processing
learningObjectives: Master the java.util.Deque double-ended interface contract across both endpoints
Analyze why legacy java.util.Stack is an architectural anti-pattern in modern Java
Implement high-performance Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stacks using Deque and ArrayDeque
Solve classic parsing and navigation algorithms (browser history, syntax validation)
expectedOutcomes: Complete technical mastery of double-ended queue operations
Ability to explain why Stack extends Vector is a classic design flaw in technical interviews

activities.title: Practical Context: Two-Way Train Tunnel vs Stack of Cafeteria Trays

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Two-Way Train Tunnel vs Stack of Cafeteria Trays
analogy.story:
Imagine a railway tunnel with open ends on both sides. Trains can enter from either East or West and exit from either East or West. This flexibility allows the tunnel to operate as a standard FIFO queue (enter East, exit West) OR as a LIFO dead-end siding (enter East, back out East).

In Java, the Deque interface provides this exact two-way capability. When constrained to only one side (push and pop at the top), it acts as a high-speed stack of cafeteria trays without the baggage of obsolete legacy synchronization.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Deque supports insertion and extraction at both ends. It unifies FIFO queue operations and modern LIFO stack operations into a single clean interface.

activities.title: Deque Architecture: Double-Ended Operations & The Modern LIFO Stack

keyTakeaways: Deque supports insertion, extraction, and inspection at both head and tail
java.util.Stack is an obsolete legacy class that extends Vector, causing severe synchronization overhead and architectural flaws
Modern Java uses Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() for all LIFO stack workloads
Deque Stack methods: push() calls addFirst(), pop() calls removeFirst(), peek() calls peekFirst()

activities.title: Browser Back-Forward Navigation Engine
activities.description: Trace a web browser history manager implementing Back and Forward buttons using two ArrayDeques.

steps.description: Initialize two ArrayDeque stacks: backStack and forwardStack.
When visiting a new URL, push currentPage to backStack and clear forwardStack.
Implement back() and forward() by pushing to one stack and popping from the other in O(1) time.

questions.question: Why is java.util.Stack considered an architectural anti-pattern in Java?
options: It extends Vector, inheriting synchronized lock overhead and exposing index methods like get(0) that break the LIFO contract
It is restricted to storing strings only
questions.explanation: Stack extends Vector, making all methods synchronized and allowing arbitrary index access (e.g. stack.get(0)), violating the LIFO abstraction.

questions.question: What is the recommended modern way to instantiate a Stack in Java?
questions.explanation: Java API documentation explicitly recommends: 'A more complete and consistent set of LIFO stack operations is provided by the Deque interface and its implementations, which should be used in preference to this class: Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<T>();'

questions.question: Which Deque method corresponds to the LIFO stack push() operation?
questions.explanation: push() inserts the element at the front of the deque (addFirst(e)), making it the top of the stack.

questions.question: What does stack.pop() do when invoked on an empty ArrayDeque?
questions.explanation: pop() calls removeFirst(), which throws a NoSuchElementException if the deque is empty. To avoid exceptions, check isEmpty() or use pollFirst() which returns null.

questions.question: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle violation in java.util.Stack.
questions.answer: Stack extends Vector, which means Stack IS-A Vector according to OOP inheritance. However, a Vector represents an indexed array where any element can be read, inserted, or removed at any index (e.g. vector.insertElementAt(item, 0)). A Stack, by definition, restricts access strictly to the top. By inheriting from Vector, Stack violates LSP because code expecting a Vector can mutate elements at arbitrary indices, destroying the Stack's internal LIFO invariants.

questions.question: How can a Deque be used to check if a string is a palindrome?
questions.answer: Insert all characters into a Deque: `for (char c : str.toCharArray()) deque.addLast(c);`. In a while loop `while (deque.size() > 1)`, call `pollFirst()` and `pollLast()`. If the characters do not match, the string is not a palindrome. If the loop completes with size 0 or 1, it is a valid palindrome. This runs in O(N) time and O(N) space.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayDeque and LinkedList when implementing a Deque?
questions.answer: ArrayDeque is backed by a circular array; LinkedList is backed by doubly-linked nodes. ArrayDeque has significantly lower memory overhead (no Node objects), superior cache locality (contiguous memory), and runs faster for both stack (push/pop) and queue (offer/poll) operations. LinkedList should only be preferred if you require concurrent removal during iteration via an active ListIterator, or need to hold null elements (which ArrayDeque prohibits).

practiceProblems.title: Verify Valid Parentheses String
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid using a Deque stack.
hints: Push opening brackets onto Deque stack.
On closing bracket, check stack.isEmpty() and compare with stack.pop().

practiceProblems.title: Palindrome Verification with Deque
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement isPalindrome(String text) using double-ended Deque operations (pollFirst and pollLast) to check if a lowercase string is a palindrome.
hints: While deque.size() > 1, compare pollFirst() and pollLast().

practiceProblems.title: Reverse String Using LIFO Stack
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a string, return the reversed string using an ArrayDeque as a LIFO stack.

practiceProblems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (tokens containing integers and '+', '-', '*', '/').
hints: For '-' and '/', note operand order: second popped is left operand, first popped is right operand.

practiceProblems.title: Simplify Unix File Path
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an absolute Unix-style file path, simplify it using a Deque stack (handling '.', '..', and duplicate slashes).
hints: If token is '..', pop from stack. If not empty and not '.', push to stack.
Read bottom to top via pollLast().
